title: How the Summa works
hookLine: objections first, then on the contrary, then I answer that, then replies

lines: IT SEEMS THAT GOD DOES NOT EXIST.
cards: It seems that God does not exist. That sentence sits in the Summa Theologiae of Thomas Aquinas, a friar and a saint who gave his life to God. He wrote it on purpose, then gave the reasons someone might say it.

If God were infinite goodness, there would be no evil, and there is evil. And nature seems able to explain itself without any God. He set out the case against his own faith, plainly, before one word in reply.
That's the method, article after article. Today's word is the book built that way.

teach.b: The Summa Theologiae is Thomas's great book of theology, and its opening lines say who it's for: beginners. So it's built to be followed one small step at a time. It's cut into questions, and each question into articles.
Every article asks one thing, as a yes or no. Whether God exists. Whether God is good.
And every article moves the same way. First, the objections. Each opens, it seems that, and gives the strongest reasons for the answer Thomas won't finally take.
He states the other side the way its friends would.
Second, on the contrary: usually one short line from a voice the Church trusts, often Scripture, sometimes an earlier teacher like Augustine. A signal that there's another side to weigh.
Third, I answer that. Now Thomas speaks for himself and gives his reasons, in order.
Fourth, the replies. He goes back to the objections one by one, often granting what's true in each before showing where it goes wrong. Nothing raised at the start is left hanging.
Some readers hear in this the debates of the medieval schools, written down. But notice what the shape asks of the writer. You can't answer an objection you've never really heard.
You have to say it well enough that the person who holds it would say, yes, that's what I mean.

teach.h: A REASON OF THAT HOPE WHICH IS IN YOU.
teach.b: The first letter of Peter gives the reason, in the Douay-Rheims: "being ready always to satisfy every one that asketh you a reason of that hope which is in you." Ready, and listening first.

how: Catholic seminaries and universities often teach students to read an article of the Summa in its four moves, objections, on the contrary, I answer that, and replies, and some use the same shape for classroom debates.

o: the sum a parish gives each year to the poor
a short prayer said at the very end of Mass
Thomas's great book, built of questions and articles

games.q: how an article moves — tap the pairs.
p: a short line from a trusted voice

s: each article of the Summa begins with Thomas's own answer
it begins with the objections, it seems that: the other side comes first.
Thomas himself wrote the sentence 'it seems that God does not exist'
it opens the objections in the article on whether God exists, which he then answers.
in the replies, Thomas skips the objections he finds weak
he goes back to the objections one by one and answers each.

games.q: you're writing a book about God for beginners. you reach the question, does God exist? what do you write first?
o: your own answer, as clearly as you can.
the strongest reasons someone might say no.
games.why: Thomas opens with the objections: it seems that God does not exist, and why. Scripture comes next, then his answer, then a reply to each objection.

practice: Bring to mind someone who disagrees with you about something that matters, and say their view silently the way Thomas would: it seems that, then their best reason and their second, in words they'd use, until you think they'd nod.
Don't answer it yet; just let their side stand, stated well. If you pray, hold that person before God for a moment.

orig.note: Latin: I answer that it must be said — the words that open Thomas's own answer in each article.

carryVoice: Your line: state the other side first. Thomas did it in every article. That's today, done.
